body: Zalloua, Z. (2024). Zahi Zalloua is Cushing Eells Professor of Philosophy and Literature and Director of IRES at Whitman College. He is also Editor of The Comparatist. His recent teaching and scholarship engage Critical Black Studies, the Posthuman, and the Palestinian Question. The politics of the wretched: Race, reason, and Ressentiment. Bloomsbury Academic, Bloomsbury Publishing Plc. // newsci dele-phant
1 Exiting the Zone of Nonbeing: The Death Drive and the Inexorable Demand for More:
The wretched are thrown into a world that
systematically de-worlds them, that
robs them of their being and agency, pushing them
further and further
into
what Frantz Fanon described as
a “zone of nonbeing.

1 They are in but not of this world.2 Or in a Heideggerian register, the wretched are (i.e., are deemed, made, or rendered) “poor in world.”3 At first blush, the torment of the zone of nonbeing is reminiscent of the existential anguish that all subjects can experience in confronting the fact of their radical freedom, their excess and irreducibility to their ego or social identity. he awareness of my nothingness—of the unnerving gap between my capacity for transcendence and the current coordinates of my substantial ego—indexes the precariousness of my being. I could be other than I am; my identity, this identity, is contingent, not necessary. his realization generates dread but also excitement at the prospect of transcending my given self, shedding my bourgeois self, and thus becoming otherwise, along with the promise of being more “authentic” insofar as I am more cognizant of my choices. But in the existing white world, Black people, Fanon notes, are unable to take advantage of this possibility for radical self-fashioning and self-determination.
While the (white) human subject enters this space of existential crisis only temporarily,
the Black
subject/
object experiences the zone of nonbeing as a suffocating cage
, a quasi- permanent condition of their desubjectivized existence.

In this chapter, I interpret the zone of nonbeing as epitomizing the condition of the wretched in a blackened world. Beginning with the zone of nonbeing emphasizes the fundamentally divided and racialized character of the world. Still, the direness of this state notwithstanding, I insist, like Fanon, on the powers of the wretched to exit this zone. While Fanon’s internationalism often leads him to frame his analysis of Blackness in more expansive terms—relating it to colonialism, imperialism, and the global structures of capitalism—Afropessimism, a vibrant movement within Critical Black Studies, has tended to limit the referential range of Blackness, restricting Fanon’s discussion to Blacks, decoupling the signifier from the wretched (which includes non- Blacks from the Global South under its umbrella).
For Afropessimists, to understand Black ressentiment you first need to understand the anti-Blackness that provokes it.
I accept this claim as axiomatic for developing a robust anti-racist politics. But what follows from this insistence on anti-Blackness is not unproblematic.
An Afropessimist refrain is that
the non-Black interlocutor will always fail to understand the gravity of anti-Blackness and the singular grammar of Black rage.
This assertion strikes me as politically self-defeating.
There is an anticipated failure, and
this failure
confirms and
justifies the Afropessimist corollary claim that cross-racial solidarity is
all but
doomed, a lure to be rejected

. The Black ressentiment that emerges under the socio-ontological condition of the zone of nonbeing, I argue, is shared by the wretched of the earth, who pass through, or rather get stuck in, the same hellish zone, as its boundaries expand in an ever-blackening world. Importantly,
Fanon did not take the zone of nonbeing to be the destiny of Black people or the wretched
, more generally—though it is experienced as such by many.
If
social death is a feature, not a bug, of an anti-Black world
, Fanon labored to understand what it would mean, and what it would take, to exit the zone of nonbeing and who/what might emerge on the other side.

This chapter continues this political and cultural labor by taking up the psychoanalytic notion of the death drive as a troubling of white futurity, driven by a Black ressentiment, sublimely translated by
Biona MacDonald’s saying, “I lives to harass white folks.”

4 For this Black civil rights activist, as critical race theorist Derrick Bell recounts, there is, strictly speaking, no hope that this world will ever change—no genuine exit from the zone of nonbeing, from what Bell names “racial realism”; MacDonald knew very well that
anti-Blackness is part of America’s cultural DNA
, but, all the same,
she did not give up on her desire for change. She used “courage and determination as weapons to … ‘harass white folks.’”
She persevered and rejoiced in unsettling white comfort.

I connect MacDonald’s life- affirming joy in white disruption, which attests to Sara Ahmed’s claim that “there can be joy in killing joy,”6 to the generative ressentiment that underpins an anti-racist politics of the death drive.

Against the numbing, repeated experience of change without change, the path of the death drive strikes at what passes for the “common” good—a notion of “common” devoid of its properly universal force, deployed to obfuscate the material interests of the powerful—exposing the political bankruptcy of society’s ideological recipes for amelioration and accommodation. It shakes the ontological foundation of the self, loosening our unconscious attachments to racial identities that insidiously reinforce our subjugation to the existing social order.
The Black Subject of the Death Drive:
The death drive is a scandal.

It is a scandal to anyone invested in the humanist subject, in the grammar of autonomy, in the Kantian ideal of a self-legislating being. To paraphrase Freud, to affirm the death drive is to willingly bring the “plague” to your field or discipline.7 It is to radicalize further Freud’s claim that “the ego is not the master in its own house.”8 The death drive—this unruly “inhuman” at the core of the human; what is in us more than us—discloses the ideal of self-mastery as nothing but a humanist distortion, a fantasy. If the death drive points to the workings of an “illogical logic”9 in human actions, what prospects does it bear for politics? Is any human(ist) endeavor invalidated from the start by this invariably corrosive idea? If not, how do you then translate the death drive’s destructive force, its undermining of the subject’s powers (over its own self-interest and well-being), into a life-affirming political vision? To put it slightly differently, what are the political stakes in avowing or disavowing the death drive? And more importantly for this chapter, what does it mean to think the death drive in relation to Black ressentiment and the zone of nonbeing?
If white society consigns Black bodies to the zone of nonbeing, exiting this zone can only remain a
phantasmatic and
ideological dream
unless there is a racial reckoning with civil society’s anti-Blackness.
Worse,
the death drive would be nothing more than a white, narcissistic indulgence in desubjectivization or self-destitution—unrelatable or foreign to Black folks
(since they are already superfluous, rendered destitute and subjectless by an inhospitable and murderous world)
and parasitical on a naturalized anti-Blackness.

Yet I believe that matters are far more ambivalent. On the one hand, a Fanonian-inflected death drive does trouble the assumption that self-destitution is available to all, an assumption grounded on the notion that identity (humanity) is available to all. On the other, it also dislocates transcendence, the “will to begin again,” as Jacques Lacan puts it, recasting the potential to exit the zone of nonbeing not as a heroic individualist endeavor but a collective cross-racial political project, what I interpret as the fruits of a public use of ressentiment. he act of entertaining the possibility of the death drive almost immediately opens up a pessimistic line of thought. It shifts the very foundations of one’s political agenda. Witness David Marriott’s objection to what he takes to be Achille Mbembe’s classical humanist commitment that “there is, in every human person, something unconquerable, fundamentally untameable, that domination—regardless of the forms it takes—cannot eliminate, nor contain, nor repress, at least not totally.”10
Against the West’s racist gaze, there is always something beneath that resists, that is irreducible to what white society tells you that you are

. Like Cedric Robinson, Mbembe is invested in recovering and amplifying a Black critical tradition—with Fanon playing a pivotal role in this anti-racist lineage. Marriott, however, proceeds to decouple Fanon from Mbembe’s humanist enlistment precisely by turning to the notion of the death drive. Marriott questions Mbembe’s identification of excess with “creative capacity,” the latter’s somewhat idealizing alignment of excess with “freedom-as-possibility”; Marriott recasts excess instead as “the lived meaning of a death drive,” which, he adds, “is also inalienable, untameable, prior to domination.”11 The death drive paints the Human in a less flattering light. What “we” share is not so much a will for freedom and/as creativity (the would-be basis for a planetary ethics, a commitment to a world in-common); rather, what we have in common is a self-sabotaging or short-circuiting foreignness from within. But Marriott is quick to tie the Freudian idea to anti-Blackness in Fanon, who understood the death drive to be “the lived meaning of black social death, a mortification which humanism can only disavow or repress.”12 Thinking the death drive in relation to anti-Blackness frames the Freudian idea in a peculiar light, compelling us to return to the subject and question its universal status and ontological make-up before fearing or celebrating its derailment. In the first pages of his introduction to Black Skin, White Masks, Fanon begins with the subject of humanism only to move to dislocate it. Fanon juxtaposes two seemingly incommensurable ideas and moods. The first comes as an implicit response to the question “Why am I writing this book?” Fanon offers his readers a list of possible reasons: Striving for a New Humanism. Understanding Mankind. Our Black Brothers. I believe in you, Man. Racial Prejudice. Understanding and Loving.13

Opening with “Striving for a New Humanism” both inscribes Fanon’s text in a humanist tradition and creates a mood of hope—hope that this new humanism might be able to redress the shortcomings of the humanist tradition, in particular its racial politics.

This is the legacy of Fanon to which Mbembe adds his name. The second passage follows a provocation to the reader. “Running the risk of angering my black brothers,” Fanon writes, “I shall say that a Black is not a man [je dirai que le Noir n’est pas un homme].” He then adds: There is a zone of nonbeing, an extraordinarily sterile and arid region, an incline stripped bare of every essential, from which a genuine new departure can emerge. In most cases, the black man cannot take advantage of this descent into a veritable hell.14
The zone of nonbeing incarnates the quasi-permanent effects of anti-Blackness;
the inferiority of Blackness gains an ontological reality.
There is seemingly
(“in most cases”)
no way out of this ontological inferno.
Black people are systematically de- worlded, zombified, denied relationality and community, stripped of individuality without the prospect of becoming something/someone else.

Their “human” capacity for transcendence—what renders legible the existentialist claim for absolute freedom, “existence precedes essence,” and the negativity of the “for itself ” (pour soi)—is indefinitely suspended.

The grammar of recognition does not belong to them nor apply to them; they don’t qualify for any dialectical upgrades (via the movement from Other to Self, modeled after Hegel’s paradigmatic Master/Slave dialectic).
As socially ostracized creatures, the blackened, the wretched, the non-recognizable, dwell in a heartless world, ostensibly sealed in their (non)being.

The rhetorical effect of setting both ideas/moods in tension from the very beginning creates a degree of interpretive uncertainty. Oscillating between optimism and pessimism, the reader ponders, What kind of “human” will this new humanism assume? And will it speak to the deadlock of the zone of nonbeing, to the “n’est pas”15 of Blackness, to the exclusion of most Black subjects from the benefits of “this descent into a veritable hell”? We can formulate Fanon’s predicament in Lacanian terms: the subject’s “descent into a veritable hell” is akin to and yet different from the experience of the Real, which is tantamount to the shattering of the subject’s symbolic identity.
The subject is caught
“between two deaths,” as Lacan puts it in the Ethics of Psychoanalysis. She is
between symbolic death and actual death: socially dead, but biologically alive.

What is at stake here is the universal status of the subject’s symbolic identity. It is precisely the givenness of identity that is absent for those racialized bodies relegated to the zone of nonbeing, cruelly subjected to the zombification of life.
The zone of nonbeing is not experienced as an ontological interruption
(a Roquentin-like nauseating experience of de trop, as Sartre might put it; an experience of the void at the core of my being)
but
, again,
as a quasi-permanent condition.
Anti-Blackness is not an aberration but an everyday structure.

We might say that the zone of nonbeing testifies to the banality of racial trauma. To assume that self-destitution (symbolic suicide— “an act of ‘losing all,’ of withdrawing from symbolic reality, that enables us to begin anew from the ‘zero point’”16) is available to all is equally to assume that identity is available to all. his assumption—shared by humanists and anti-humanists alike—can reinforce an anti-Black world insofar as the human as such is ironically let under- theorized, divorced from Western modernity’s political ontology, its racial and colonial projects: its disciplining and categorizing of bodies as human, not-quite-human, and nonhuman.17 The death drive is directly implicated in this discussion to the extent that it is also preoccupied with self-destitution and human agency. Commenting on the death drive’s relation to the zone of nonbeing, Derek Hook vigorously affirms that it is “perhaps only with reference to this conceptual supplement [the death drive] that we are able to properly grasp the revolutionary potential [of the] idea of the zone of nonbeing.”18 Hook is relying here on the Lacanian inflection of the death drive as ethical cause, as contrasted with the Freudian death instinct.19 he Lacanian death drive as a fidelity to a cause—as embodied in Antigone’s heroic resistance to King Creon’s cruel authority— recasts the zone of nonbeing as a project straddling the ethical and the political. In this light, the death drive as an engine of change is poised to enable the Black subject to finally take advantage of this descent into a veritable hell and fashion or recreate itself anew. But the same lingering question remains: as with the alleged givenness of symbolic identity, what is the universal force of the death drive in an anti-Black world? he fact that Fanon says “in most cases” rather than “in all cases” the Black man cannot take advantage of his situation opens up the possibility that this zone of nonbeing is not a fully totalized space. his zone of nonbeing—the n’est pas or condition of Black social death—is not destiny. he death drive is another way to imagine the ontological incompleteness of the Black subject. It registers a gap between the empty subject of psychoanalysis and the social ego. Is harnessing the negativity of the death drive then a viable means to transcend the zone of nonbeing? The question hinges of course on how we understand transcendence.
If society effortlessly relegates Black bodies to the zone of nonbeing,
exiting this zone remains an ideological fantasy unless civil society’s anti-Blackness is effectively dealt with

(the same holds for the idea of a “new humanism”). Transcendence here must be stripped of its existentialist and individualist residue. Exiting the zone of nonbeing—and/as inaugurating a new humanism—will be a collective effort or it will not be. Fanon’s evocation of “descent” rather than the more typical existentialist language of transcendence signals the author’s skepticism about the privilege and powers of transcendence in an anti-Black world.20
Thinking with the death drive
in a world where zones of nonbeing exist shits the focus away from the vagaries of individual transcendence and
sends us back to civil society’s
collective unconscious, to its
anti-Black libidinal economy: the implicit rules and principles regulating desires and fears, the production, circulation, and consumption of anti-Blackness.
A given society’s libidinal economy governs our deep sense of who affectively matters
, belongs, and counts—
and who effectively doesn’t.

This is as true for Black as it is for whites, since experiencing oneself as a phobic object deeply impacts one’s self-worth. Politicizing the death drive then calls for a reckoning with the racist symbolic order and the collective unconscious underpinning it. I want to return now to Fanon’s remark that “a Black is not a man.” Fanon notes the provocative character of this claim, stating, “At the risk of arousing the ressentiment of my colored brothers, I will say that the black is not a man”21 (“Dussé-je encourir le ressentiment de mes frères de couleur, je dirai que le Noir n’est pas un homme”22). Though the main point that Fanon seems to be stressing here is the negative emotion that he is expecting from his Black interlocutors, the fact that he chooses the Nietzschean register of ressentiment (and not colère or rage, for instance) might not be irrelevant, especially if we examine further the object of ire: the statement that the Black man is not a man. Fanon anticipates that his interlocutors will read this assertion as a slight, a denigration of their being and a denial that they are worthy of claiming the universal or Republican ideal of the human subject—that they don’t belong to this “order of reality.”23 heir ressentiment is a “reaction” to Fanon’s critique. Again, to be reactional characterizes the Nietzschean “man of ressentiment.” Later in Black Skin, White Masks, Fanon makes explicit the Nietzschean insight that “there is always ressentiment in reaction,”24 before approvingly quoting Nietzsche’s posthumous he Will to Power: “To induce man to be actional, by maintaining in his circularity the respect of the fundamental values that make the world human, that is the task of utmost urgency for he who, after careful reflection, prepares to act.”25 Fanon imagines his interlocutors not as acting, but precisely as reacting to his observation. heir protestation would take the form of a correction to his distortion: the Black man is a man (le Noir est un homme). In other words, their ressentiment fuels their preservation of their being—the claim that they are human too. Ressentiment, in this instance, is about defending identity and laying claim to the human of Western civilization. What Fanon’s hasty readers miss is the full force of his critique. Fanon’s aim is clearly not to denigrate his Black brethren, but to expose the social phantasm that passes for the human, their narcissistic investments in the solidity of their internalized and projected identity. Fanon makes this point obliquely when he says that “the black man wants to be white” (and thus is in part responsible for his own alienation), but also adds, “
the white man is desperately trying to achieve the rank of man
[une condition d’homme].”26 In this rank-ordering of human beings, the white man is not a man either, in the absolute sense of the term—no empirical human being is.
The pure human is a socio-political fantasy undergirding the being of whiteness as well as the nothingness
(n’est pas)
of Blackness
. The grammar of the Human has thus everything to do with racial power and the regulation of desires and attachments.

Forging a new grammar, which would necessarily entail a new ontology (since language both reflects and shapes being), is the daunting challenge facing the wretched, the blackened subject of modernity. “In the world I am heading for,” Fanon affirms, “I am endlessly creating myself.”27
Without reinventing grammar and ontology, a genuine new departure from the zone of nonbeing can never emerge, let alone be imagined.
